chief_complaint: sudden difficulty breathing, hives, and shock immediately upon receiving a blood transfusion
hpi_details: 28F with asymptomatic baseline IgA deficiency (<7 mg/dL) and anti-IgA antibodies experiencing acute anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of starting a packed red blood cell transfusion.
ideas: She thinks the hospital accidentally mixed up her chart and hooked her up to the wrong blood type.
concerns: She is worried that the foreign blood entering her veins could permanently damage her organs or stop her heart.
expectations: She hopes the medical team can immediately give her an antidote to reverse the reaction and flush the donor blood out with IV fluids.
pmh: Selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies; hypertension, mild dyslipidemia

clinical_knowledge.topic: Anaphylactic Transfusion Reaction (IgA deficiency) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Anaphylactic Transfusion Reaction (IgA deficiency) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management is immediate cessation of the transfusion plus standard anaphylaxis treatment (IM epinephrine), with washed or IgA-deficient blood products required for any future transfusions, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden difficulty breathing, hives, and shock immediately upon receiving a blood transfusion
Key HPI features: 28F with asymptomatic baseline IgA deficiency (<7 mg/dL) and anti-IgA antibodies experiencing acute anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of starting a packed red blood cell transfusion.

Objective/Exam findings: Hypotension and tachycardia with diffuse urticaria and respiratory distress beginning within 10 minutes of transfusion start; no fever or hemoglobinuria to suggest a hemolytic reaction.
Relevant background/PMH: Selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies; hypertension, mild dyslipidemia
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Anaphylactic Transfusion Reaction (IgA deficiency).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Symptom onset within minutes of the transfusion starting.
management_principles: Immediately stop the transfusion and treat as anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine; use washed or IgA-deficient blood products for any future transfusion
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Selective IgA Deficiency Anaphylactic Transfusion Reaction: sudden difficulty breathing, hives, and shock immediately upon receiving a blood transfusion. 28F with asymptomatic baseline IgA deficiency (<7 mg/dL) and anti-IgA antibodies experiencing acute anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of starting a packed red blood cell transfusion.
reference_soap.objective: Hypotension and tachycardia with diffuse urticaria and respiratory distress beginning within 10 minutes of transfusion start; no fever or hemoglobinuria to suggest a hemolytic reaction.
reference_soap.assessment: Anaphylactic transfusion reaction secondary to anti-IgA antibodies in a patient with selective IgA deficiency.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Immediately stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with normal saline. 2. Treat as anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine, oxygen, and further supportive care per standard anaphylaxis protocol. 3. Notify the blood bank of the reaction; for any future transfusion, use washed red cells, IgA-deficient blood products, or blood from IgA-deficient donors. 4. Refer to allergy/immunology and confirm anti-IgA antibody status.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Selective IgA Deficiency Anaphylactic Transfusion Reaction
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for sudden difficulty breathing, hives, and shock immediately upon receiving a blood transfusion
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for allergy_immunology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: In a patient with selective IgA deficiency, anti-IgA antibodies attack donor IgA in transfused blood, causing anaphylaxis within minutes of the transfusion starting.
red_flags: Symptom onset within minutes of the transfusion starting
Hypotension or airway symptoms during transfusion

must_ask.say: How soon after the transfusion started did you feel unwell?

must_ask.objective: Known IgA deficiency or prior transfusion reactions
must_ask.say: Have you ever been told you have low IgA, or reacted to a transfusion before?
What symptoms did you have — hives, breathing trouble, feeling faint?
Do you know what type of blood product you were receiving?
Does anyone in your family have a known IgA deficiency or recurrent infections?

history.answer: I was receiving a blood transfusion a few minutes ago, and suddenly I couldn't catch my breath and broke out in itchy hives.
It started out of nowhere about ten minutes after the nurse began infusing the blood.
It feels terrible and suffocating, even while I am just lying completely still in bed.
It came on very fast and has stayed severe, and I have never experienced anything like this before.
Lying flat makes it even harder to breathe, but this didn't happen while I was sleeping.
It happened specifically during the blood transfusion, not from cold air, dust, exercise, or foods.
Yes, my throat feels like it is closing up and I can hear a high-pitched wheezing sound when I breathe.
I don't have a cough or phlegm, and I definitely don't have a fever or chills.
My chest feels very tight and constricted, but there is no sharp stabbing pain when I take a breath.
My heart is pounding very fast, and I feel lightheaded and dizzy like I might faint.
No, I haven't coughed up any blood at all.
No, my legs are not swollen and my weight hasn't changed recently.
Neither calf is painful or swollen, and I haven't been on any long flights or bed rest.
I was getting blood because severe heavy periods made me extremely anemic and exhausted, but I have no stomach bleeding.
My lips and fingers feel a little numb, and I feel very panicked because I can hardly breathe.
I don't have asthma, COPD, or heart disease, and I have never used an inhaler.
I don't take aspirin, ibuprofen, beta-blockers, or any allergy medications.
The nurse told me they were giving me one bag of packed red blood cells.
Large red, itchy bumps broke out all over my face, chest, and arms right as my breathing got difficult.
No, my urine has looked completely normal, not dark, red, or brown.
No, I have no pain in my lower back or sides.
I have never received any blood transfusions before today.
A doctor once mentioned that I have selective IgA deficiency, but I never had any symptoms from it before.
Aside from the selective IgA deficiency, I have high blood pressure and slightly elevated cholesterol.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink alcohol socially, having maybe one or two glasses of wine a month.
I work full-time in an office as an administrator, and I live with my husband.
My mother was also diagnosed with selective IgA deficiency, but no one in my family has severe allergies.
My last period started three weeks ago; my cycles are heavy, but we use condoms and my pregnancy test was negative.
I thought the nurses must have given me the wrong blood type by mistake because my body rejected it instantly.
I'm terrified that this donor blood is poisoning my body or going to cause permanent organ damage before it clears out.
I just need an emergency shot to stop this reaction right now and for someone to double-check that my blood type wasn't mixed up.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, pulse is 126 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 89% on room air, and body temperature is 36.8°C.
Patient is in acute respiratory distress with visible intercostal retractions, accessory muscle use, diaphoresis, and no digital clubbing.
Conjunctivae demonstrate mild pallor bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Mild pharyngeal and uvular edema present without tonsillar enlargement; oral mucosa is pale.
Jugular veins are flat without signs of distension.
Percussion note is normal and resonant symmetrically across all lung fields.
Diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezing and mild inspiratory stridor are heard; no coarse crackles or focal consolidation.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal heart sounds with no murmurs, gallops, friction rubs, or third heart sound.
Diffuse erythematous urticarial plaques and wheals are present across the face, chest, abdomen, and all four extremities.
No peripheral pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Calves are symmetric without unilateral swelling, warmth, erythema, or tenderness.
